name: Light Brownish Drab
lede: Light Brownish Drab is a muted reddish tan from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, close enough to Pale Taupe and Warm Grey that the three are hard to tell apart on screen.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone, two near-twins
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate XLV, hue 9″″ [1]. The Inter-Society Color Council's 1955 dictionary filed the same tone under block 60, naming it light grayish brown, 4.8 units from Ridgway's original reading [1].

In our color library its two closest neighbors are [[pale-taupe]] and [[warm-grey]], each about 3.4 units away, a gap small enough that most viewers would call all three the same color [2]. [[light-cinnamon-drab]] sits a little further off, about 4.5 units away and visibly more yellow [2]. [[cinereous]] is about 4.8 units away, darker and redder [2]. The name itself is a modifier chain built from Ridgway's drab family rather than a word chosen for its own associations [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 512 of them, about 2.15 percent, as photographed, making it more common than 76 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 4.0 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 2.5 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [3].

Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, in 33 percent of its 295 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [3]. The Danish painter Fritz Syberg favors it most, in 5 of the 13 of his works in the archive, 6.1 times his museums' baseline rate [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment identification [3].
